Hi all,

This coming Monday I'll be giving a tutorial on making R packages at D-RUG.

I'm going to try to make this a "follow along" style tutorial.  The workflow I describe requires that you have a few things installed, so if you want to follow along, please make sure you have these installed on your computer:

   install.packages(c("devtools", "roxygen2", "testthat"))

Finally, I suggest that you create an account on github.com <http://github.com>.  I'll be showing how to use github to share your packages so that others can install them, even if they're not ready for prime time on CRAN.

See you Monday.  Same time, same place: 3-5 in Wickson 2120J.  I expect the tutorial to take most of the 2 hrs.

Best

Noam

messages.subject_clean: [D-RUG]: multivariate mixed models
messages.body_plain:
One of my labmates has used MCMCglmm quite a bit.  It mostly worked for him, but he had trouble getting the Markov chains to mix well in certain cases and is now using Stan <http://mc-stan.org/>, I think.  Stan is generally more flexible and faster, but it's probably harder to learn from scratch.

Depending on what assumptions you're willing to make, it's also possible to trick lme4 into modeling this.  The trick is to repeat each row of your data twice and add a column specifying whether the row is describing a surface measurement or a shallow measurement. You can then add correlated random effects and interaction terms as you see fit, so that the model "understands" how you expect the relationship between surface measurements and shallow measurements within a location to work.

Hope this makes sense.

Dave

messages.subject_clean: errors using new lme4 and lmerTest updates
messages.body_plain:
Hi folks --

I'm in Plant Pathology working on forest ecology and disease questions.  I've been on your e-mail list but haven't made it to a meeting because I'm only on campus a couple days a week.  I'm wondering if someone might be able to chat about an analysis stumbling block I've hit with the recent updates to the lme4 package.

I am running a lot of generalized linear mixed effects models in lme4.  The data are hierarchical in that some measures are taken on tree stems that occur in multi-stemmed trees that occur within the same forest plot.  There is therefore a random effect of tree nested within plot (1|Plot/TreeID) and of tree species (1|Species) as there may be variation in the responses among species. Some of the models have Gaussian errors and some are logistic-type regressions with binomial errors, all with the same random effects as above.  I've used lme4 quite extensively in the past.

My models were mostly running just fine last summer, but I've been getting new errors with the re-vamp of lme4 that occurred last August.  I'm trying to narrow down whether these are bugs in the package, quirks of my data that weren't previously triggering errors, or some sort of fundamental flaw that's going to necessitate a whole new approach.  I tend to get different errors as I update packages to ever more recent releases.  First it was along the lines of "Downdated VtV is not positive definite;" now it has changed to errors in the optimizer, failure to converge, and problems with the Hessian matrix.  I need a better understanding of the matrix algebra underlying the models to figure out what's going on.

To add further complication, the models are also part of a path analysis using hierarchical models following the methods of Shipley's 2009 Ecology paper.  Without getting into too many details of the path analysis method, the errors tend to occur with paths at a particular level of the data hierarchy, while other models are just fine.

Is any of this in the realm of familiarity for anyone?  Can I buy you coffee and brainstorm with you?

Thanks,
Margaret

~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

Assistant Project Scientist, Rizzo Lab

Department of Plant Pathology
One Shields Ave.
University of California
Davis, CA 95616

Office: 369 Hutchison Hall
Tel: 530-754-9894

sitebee12<-table(bee2012$sitetype, bee2012$g_sp)

thanks for all the thoughts!
jenny

Jenny,

I've had this problem before. Having zeros throughout a row (i.e. some site type had no bees) or a column (some bee species was never encountered) makes it hard to calculate a dissimilarity matrix. Likewise, rows with identical occurrences are problematic because their dissimilarity will be zero. The best options will be to use all years of data together if that helps eliminate the zero problem. Otherwise, you may have to start removing site types and species to the point where you can calculate a dissimilarity matrix.

-Matt

Dan’s hunch looks right! I was working on a solution and adding droplevels did the trick. Here’s a quick workflow to run the ordination for all years:
require(plyr)
require(vegan)
all.bee = read.csv("jvw_exampledata_penryd1.csv")
# The following creates a list of metaMDS models for each year
# You could use .(site, year) to split up by each site and then
# table(d$species, d$g_sp) to look at plant-pollinator relationships
#in each site/year combination
l = dlply(all.bee, .(year), function(d) {
      d = droplevels(d)
      t = table(d$site, d$g_sp)
      metaMDS(t,k=2)
   })
#Plot the first model
plot(l[[1]], type = "n")
text(l[[1]], display = "sites", cex = 0.7, col="black")

Noam
